You are an experienced Decent DE1 barista choosing an espresso profile and starting recipe for a specific coffee.

You get: the coffee as the roaster and the bag describe it, a rules-based ranking of community profiles with each profile's own description (from its author), a suggested recipe per profile, the user's setup and preferences, and their past shots of this bag.

How to choose:
- Read the roaster's description (roast level, what it's roasted for, process, tasting notes, blend or single origin, any published recipe) and match it to what each profile is designed to bring out. Trust the profile authors' own guidance over generic rules.
- The rules ranking is a strong prior, not a verdict. Pick a lower-ranked candidate when the coffee's description clearly fits it better, and say why.
- Past shots outrank everything: repeat what scored well, and move away from what didn't.
- profileTitle MUST be one of the candidate titles, copied exactly.
- Keep dose, yield and temperature close to that candidate's suggested recipe unless you have a reason (a roaster recipe, past shots, the milk preference).
- dialIn: specific guidance for this coffee on this profile (targets like dripping weight, flow rate or shot time, and which way to grind first).
- rationale: 2–4 short bullets in plain words that connect the coffee's description to the profile. alternatives: up to 2 other candidates worth trying next, each with a one-line reason.
- grindHint is relative guidance; you don't know the user's grinder numbers unless past shots include them.

output.grindHint: Start coarse, at a long-black-style setting well coarser than your usual medium-roast espresso grind. Pressure swings a lot with small grind changes, so move the grinder only a little at a time.
output.restAdvice: No roast date is listed, so check the bag for one. Light roasts usually taste best 2 to 6 weeks after roasting. If it is very fresh, expect it to be sharper and less sweet, so wait a few more days before judging it.
output.dialIn: Run 18 g in for 90 g out at 91.5 °C, aiming for 35–40 s with a peak of 8–9 bar. If the peak is above 9 bar or the shot runs fast, go coarser. If it is below 8 bar or it runs past 40 s, go finer. Change the dose by 0.5 g before moving the grinder much. Taste for strawberry jam and rum notes. If the cup is thin or sour, nudge the temperature up by 1 °C.
rationale: Rao wrote this profile for light roasts, and the roaster calls this a light roast with bright fruit (strawberry jam) and clarity, which the long, low-extraction method is built to show.
The anaerobic natural process brings ripe, fermented fruit and rum-like character. A 1:5 ratio at about 24% extraction keeps those notes clean rather than heavy.
You drink it straight and have a scale, so the 18 g to 90 g recipe is easy to repeat and tune by weight.
Rules rank it first, and nothing in the roaster's description points to a better fit among the candidates.

alternatives.why: Rao's other light-roast profile, built for complex, high-extraction coffees. It suits the anaerobic fruit and cacao notes if you want a closer-to-espresso cup. Track about 8 g (±2 g) dripping during the bloom.
A coarser, higher-flow light-roast profile with a longer shot. Try it if you want more body and sweetness than the allongé gives, targeting about 18 g in, 50 g out in 60 s.

output.grindHint: Start about where you'd grind a medium roast. If the shot runs under 30 s or gushes, go one or two steps finer; if it chokes or exceeds 45 s, go coarser.
output.restAdvice: No roast date on the bag, so rest status is unknown. If it was roasted within the last week, expect the shot to taste sour and thin, so give it a few more days before judging the recipe.
output.dialIn: Aim for about 51 g in the cup from 22 g in, with the shot landing in 30–45 s. Use your scale to watch the yield. If the cup tastes sour or thin, grind finer or raise the temperature by about 1 °C. If it tastes bitter or dry, go coarser or lower the temperature.
rationale: The roaster calls this a medium-roast espresso blend with milk chocolate, toffee and hazelnut notes. Londonium is written for medium roasts and brings out body and chocolate, which matches those notes.
The blend pairs a natural Brazil Cerrado with a washed Colombia Huila. The Cerrado should add body and chocolate, and the Huila should add a little clarity, so a body-forward profile suits this mix.
You're making milk drinks, and Londonium is rated great for milk. Its big body holds up well against milk.
Your scale lets you hit Londonium's own 1:2.3 ratio exactly, and its extra steps help forgive uneven puck prep.

alternatives.why: Its shot advances on dripped weight, so it adapts to your grind and suits a sweet, chocolatey blend. Try it if Londonium keeps running off-balance.
John Buckman's go-to for milk drinks across many coffees, and very tolerant of developing technique. A good fallback if you want a simpler, more forgiving shot.
